title: Lecture 15. Research Design and Evidence-Based Prevention
summary:
1 Evidence-Based

2 Main Types of Research Design

3 “Scientists Have Proven”

1. Evidence-Based What distinguishes a good doctor? Probably everyone would agree that, first and foremost, it's extensive professional experience. The more patients a doctor observes, the more connections form in their mind between symptoms and possible treatments. From their own experience, they see which treatments are effective in which cases, and which are not.

But the problem is that the human brain is not very well adapted to generalizations and objective judgments; it is geared towards building simple hypotheses necessary for survival. If we found mushrooms in the forest somewhere last time, then we should look there again next time. If a fish bit in a certain spot or on a certain bait, next time we should cast our rod there again with the same bait. And the more our positive experience finds confirmation, the more stable our hypotheses become. But this also increases the likelihood that we increasingly begin to ignore more mushroom-rich or fish-rich spots than those we focused on. Skinner demonstrated how easily such connections form in our minds in his famous experiments, which became a crucial contribution to the development of behaviorism. Returning to our doctor: their extensive professional experience alone cannot guarantee a sufficiently objective view on the treatment of various problems. A good doctor can become a prisoner of their own hypotheses, "implicit theories," and overlook other more effective possibilities. This very problem once acutely faced the healthcare system – the lack of objective criteria for choosing the most effective treatment method, especially in situations where different doctors had different opinions on the same problem. A methodology was needed that would allow for an objective and unambiguous answer in situations of choosing a treatment or prevention method.

2. Main Types of Research Design As mentioned in the lesson on experiments, it is the most reliable method for testing the relationship between factorial and outcome variables. In a simple mechanical system, an experiment can easily demonstrate: a) the connection between phenomena, and b) the cause-and-effect direction of this connection. For example, if we repeatedly throw a stone into water, ripples will spread across the water's surface each time, immediately after the stone hits the water. However, in behavioral and social systems, conducting such a pure experiment is impossible because, due to the complexity of human behavior, there will be too many unaccounted factors in our experimental situation that can uncontrollably influence the result. Therefore, in medicine and social sciences, their own methodological techniques have emerged, allowing research design to approximate an experiment. Let's consider several key concepts of this methodology.

Cross-sectional (or single-point) studies

Cross-sectional studies – participants are surveyed once, after a program has taken place and its effect has occurred. This is the simplest and therefore frequently used research design option in social sciences. It is convenient for a single-point assessment of the prevalence of a certain characteristic in the studied sample, but unreliable for testing cause-and-effect relationships, because such a research plan looks to the past, and the researcher relies on respondents' memory of events that have already happened, and which they are not always able to accurately recall and evaluate.

For example, we want to study the impact of a preventive program aimed at reducing smoking among students. Below is a theoretical diagram of such a research plan. The red figure is the researcher, positioned on the right, which means they conduct the study after the factorial variable (in our case, the preventive program) has occurred, and when the supposed effect of this program – a decrease in smoking levels among students – has followed. In such a situation, the researcher can only study past experience, relying on the memory and words of the subjects.

Longitudinal studies, where the same participants are surveyed more than once at different time points, are a more reliable method for testing cause-and-effect relationships because the researcher has better control over the research subject.

Cohort studies – a form of longitudinal study in which the same group of people (a cohort), united by some common characteristic: illness/disorder, age, or experience, is studied over time. For example, people born in the same year form an age cohort.

“Case-Control”

The "Case-Control" research design is stronger than a cross-sectional study. Here, the "researcher" is positioned to the left of the "outcome" of the preventive program. This means that, in our example, they determine the fact of smoking among students after the preventive program has taken place, using some objective, reliable method (e.g., express tests for nicotine content in breath or urine), rather than simply relying on students' words about their smoking experience, as was the case in the previous research plan. However, the researcher still cannot precisely determine which students participated in the preventive program, except by their own accounts.

"Cases" here refer to students who fall into a risk group, for example, because they continue to smoke after the program. "Controls" here refer to "healthy" students who do not smoke after the program (though we do not know if they smoked before it).

The black font of the inscription "Outcome Variable" means that the researcher starts by defining student cohorts based on the outcome variable — smoking frequency, i.e., the supposed result of the preventive program. Then, these groups are divided into those who participated in the program ("Exposure present" — exposed), and those who did not participate ("Exposure absent" — unexposed).

Cohort Studies: Retrospective and Prospective

Cohort studies are longitudinal studies where the same group of people (a cohort), united by some common characteristic: illness/disorder, age, or experience, is studied more than once. For example, people born in the same year form an age cohort. This is a more reliable method for testing cause-and-effect relationships because the researcher has better control over the research subject, both at the factorial variable stage and at the outcome variable stage.

A retrospective cohort study is similar to a "case-control" study, but our researcher already knows exactly which students participated in the preventive program and which did not (which is why the words "Factorial Variable" in the diagram are written in black, and the dark lines do not "mix" as before, but run parallel to each other). However, merely knowing this is not enough! To correctly compare these two groups — experimental and control — they must be formed initially, adhering to a randomization procedure. Therefore, the analysis is still conducted retrospectively: first, students are divided into "Healthy" and "Risk Group," meaning those who did not smoke and those who smoked, for example, in the last week. Then, within these, groups are identified of those who participated in our preventive program and those who did not (which is why the gray arrows in the diagram point to the past).

Such a retrospective plan is stronger than a "case-control" study in terms of evidence, but it does not allow for determining a cause-and-effect relationship and proving that students stopped smoking specifically as a result of our program, and not due to any other factors. To prove this, the researcher needs to:

a) Objectively and reliably determine the prevalence of smoking among students BEFORE and AFTER the program (e.g., using express tests);

b) Ensure complete randomness when assigning students to the group that will participate in the program (experimental group) and the others (control group).

Why is this important? Because to prove the program's effectiveness, the researcher needs to answer two questions:

a) did the level of smoking among students in the experimental group change (decrease) after the program's intervention?

b) did the level of smoking among students in the control group change (decrease) during the same period?

The program is effective only if the smoking level decreased in the experimental group, but not in the control group!

And the randomization procedure when forming experimental and control groups is necessary to exclude the influence of any other factors besides the evaluated program.

To answer these questions convincingly, a Prospective Cohort Study procedure is necessary, where the researcher initially has full control over the situation. The gray arrows in the diagram, pointing to the "future," indicate the logic of the analysis, which begins with dividing into experimental and control groups, and then within them — into "Healthy" and "Risk Group." These groups are then compared with the measurements of smoking prevalence that the researcher took BEFORE the program.

3. “Scientists Have Proven” We often hear the phrase “scientists have proven” or “as studies have shown”… What truly lies behind these phrases?

One can speak of evidential strength when conditions are met at three levels of research:

  • Optimal research methods have been selected,
  • An optimal research design has been chosen, i.e., the procedures for applying these research methods,
  • The results of similar studies have been generalized and shown their consistency in a Systematic Review.

The main idea of the evidence-based methodology can be represented as the "pyramid of evidence-based medicine." On it, from bottom to top by degree of evidential strength, are the types of research designs we discussed above.

Systematic reviews represent the pinnacle of evidential strength – the results of generalizations from numerous studies published in peer-reviewed journals. Typically, Systematic reviews are based on meta-analysis — a quantitative statistical processing of data from various studies dedicated to a single topic.

Systematic reviews are published in special libraries that have "Systematic reviews" sections. In them, one can find descriptions of research results on a vast number of problems, not only purely medical ones but also socio-medical and psychological issues related to prevention in the education system. The most famous of these libraries, Cochrane, is supported by an international non-profit organization, named after Archibald Cochrane, which studies the effectiveness of treatment methods using evidence-based medicine, and publishes systematic reviews, primarily of randomized controlled trials, in its database — the Cochrane Library.

Statistics, as a science, became the methodological basis for solving these problems. Its application in medicine was substantiated by the Scottish epidemiologist

Archibald Cochrane (Archibald Cochrane, 1909–1988), who is called the father of evidence-based medicine. In 1972, Cochrane published his famous book titled “Effectiveness and Efficiency: Random Reflections on Health Services,” which marked a new page in the history of the healthcare system.
